title: Disk Latency and I/O Performance (Windows)
exclusions: Detects a Windows logical-disk instance whose `Avg. Disk sec/Read` or `Avg. Disk sec/Write` one-minute average exceeds 25 milliseconds in two consecutive complete one-minute buckets. A pair is locally classified critical when either minute exceeds 50 milliseconds. These values implement Microsoft Windows Server's published general warning (>25 ms), critical (>50 ms), and investigate-over-one-minute guidance; they are not storage-vendor service levels or universal application-impact guarantees. The rule converts only the two seconds-per-operation latency counters to milliseconds. It does not convert `Current Disk Queue Length`, rates, bytes, percentages, or free-space values as latency. `_Total` is excluded so each result identifies a logical volume. This rule does not diagnose the cause, prove physical-disk failure, identify an I/O-producing process, measure SAN/virtual-storage internals, predict capacity, or establish an outage. PhysicalDisk, Storage Spaces, CSV, ReFS/NTFS integrity, free space, queue depth, throughput, IOPS, split I/O, application response time, and storage-vendor telemetry are supporting or separate contracts. Missing counters, hosts, volumes, samples, or delayed forwarding are collection-health failures, not healthy storage. The fixed index, five-minute delayed window, two-bucket persistence, and local severity are implementation choices. No process, disk, volume, application, VM, storage array, or failover action is performed and no compliance claim is made.
evidence: After deployment, retain authoritative Windows host, logical-volume, application/service, virtualization, and storage ownership inventory; the approved `inputs.conf` Perfmon stanza and deployment-server revision; Windows and Splunk counter-name/locale verification; representative raw `Perfmon:LogicalDisk` samples; independent host/input/sample-delay and field-completeness health; version-controlled `windows_logical_disk_sustained_latency` search, ACL, schedule, dispatch history, and result rows; dashboard and runbook revisions; storage/application incident or change disposition; and dated positive, negative, threshold-boundary, persistence, missing-sample, duplicate-route, delayed-data, `_Total`, null-field, and counter-unit tests. Preserve host, instance, counter, raw seconds, derived milliseconds, minute buckets, consecutive-pair times, event/index delay, storage mapping, workload context, and source-health state under approved retention. This documentation-only review created no Windows counter sample, Splunk input, lookup, alert, dashboard, incident, storage diagnosis, or production validation evidence.

controlTest.positiveScenario: In a fixed complete five-minute test window, ingest `Perfmon:LogicalDisk` samples for `host=server01.example`, `instance=D:`, and both exact latency counter names at a validated interval. Create two adjacent minute buckets whose read averages are 0.026 and 0.027 seconds; expect one warning row with a 27 ms peak. Repeat with adjacent write averages of 0.051 and 0.052 seconds; expect one critical row with a 52 ms peak. Assert endpoint, volume, pair times, read/write sample counts, raw-to-ms conversion, severity, thresholds, event/index timing, and UC ID.
controlTest.negativeScenario: Expect zero rows when all minute averages are <=25 ms; when a value equals exactly 25 ms; when only one minute exceeds 25 ms; when two breached minutes are separated by a minute; for `_Total`; for `Current Disk Queue Length`, `Disk Transfers/sec`, or any non-latency counter; for wrong source/sourcetype, blank host/instance, nonnumeric/negative Value, events outside the closed window, or a duplicate sample. A 50 ms pair is warning because critical is strictly >50 ms. Separate health results must expose a missing expected host/counter/minute, delayed data, locale drift, duplicate route, and malformed sample rather than treating absence as good performance.

dataSources: Primary data is Windows Performance Data Helper output collected by a local Splunk Enterprise or Universal Forwarder Perfmon input and normalized by Splunk Add-on for Microsoft Windows: `index=perfmon`, `source=Perfmon:LogicalDisk` or `sourcetype=Perfmon:LogicalDisk`, exact `counter` values `Avg. Disk sec/Read` and `Avg. Disk sec/Write`, logical-disk `instance`, numeric `Value` in seconds, `host`, `_time`, and `_indextime`. Configure `object=LogicalDisk`, `instances=*`, an owner-approved interval no greater than 60 seconds, and `useEnglishOnly=true` where supported so the exact English counter contract is stable. Supporting counters include `Avg. Disk sec/Transfer`, `Disk Reads/sec`, `Disk Writes/sec`, `Disk Read Bytes/sec`, `Disk Write Bytes/sec`, `Avg. Disk Queue Length`, `Current Disk Queue Length`, and process I/O operations; use PhysicalDisk, Windows/storage event logs, application telemetry, hypervisor/cloud/storage-array metrics, and vendor limits for diagnosis.
app: Splunk Add-on for Microsoft Windows (`Splunk_TA_windows`, Splunkbase 742) supplies supported Perfmon logical-disk sourcetypes, extractions, and Performance CIM mappings. A Windows forwarder performs local collection through the Splunk Perfmon input; Universal Forwarder is a Splunk product, not Splunkbase app 617. A local observability app owns the saved search, source-health checks, dashboard, tests, routing, and runbook.
spl:
index=perfmon (source="Perfmon:LogicalDisk" OR sourcetype="Perfmon:LogicalDisk") counter IN ("Avg. Disk sec/Read","Avg. Disk sec/Write") earliest=-10m@m latest=-5m@m
| eval endpoint=lower(trim(host)), volume=lower(trim(instance)), sample_value=tonumber(Value)
| where len(endpoint)>0 AND endpoint!="-" AND len(volume)>0 AND volume!="-" AND volume!="_total" AND isnotnull(sample_value) AND sample_value>=0
| dedup _time endpoint volume counter sample_value
| eval latency_ms=sample_value*1000
| bin _time span=1m
| stats avg(eval(if(counter="Avg. Disk sec/Read",latency_ms,null()))) as read_latency_ms avg(eval(if(counter="Avg. Disk sec/Write",latency_ms,null()))) as write_latency_ms count(eval(if(counter="Avg. Disk sec/Read",1,null()))) as read_samples count(eval(if(counter="Avg. Disk sec/Write",1,null()))) as write_samples min(_indextime) as first_index_time max(_indextime) as last_index_time by _time endpoint volume
| eval minute_peak_ms=case(isnotnull(read_latency_ms) AND isnotnull(write_latency_ms),max(read_latency_ms,write_latency_ms),isnotnull(read_latency_ms),read_latency_ms,isnotnull(write_latency_ms),write_latency_ms)
| where minute_peak_ms>25
| sort 0 endpoint volume _time
| streamstats current=f window=1 last(_time) as previous_breach_time last(minute_peak_ms) as previous_peak_ms by endpoint volume
| where _time-previous_breach_time=60
| eval pair_peak_ms=max(minute_peak_ms,previous_peak_ms), pair_severity=if(pair_peak_ms>50,"critical","warning")
| stats min(previous_breach_time) as breach_start max(_time) as breach_end max(pair_peak_ms) as peak_latency_ms avg(read_latency_ms) as avg_read_latency_ms avg(write_latency_ms) as avg_write_latency_ms sum(read_samples) as read_samples sum(write_samples) as write_samples values(pair_severity) as observed_severities min(first_index_time) as first_index_time max(last_index_time) as last_index_time by endpoint volume
| eval local_severity=if(peak_latency_ms>50,"critical","warning"), warning_threshold_ms=25, critical_threshold_ms=50, persistence_minutes=2, use_case="UC-1.2.104", breach_start_utc=strftime(breach_start,"%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ"), breach_end_utc=strftime(breach_end+60,"%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ")
| table endpoint volume local_severity peak_latency_ms avg_read_latency_ms avg_write_latency_ms read_samples write_samples breach_start_utc breach_end_utc first_index_time last_index_time warning_threshold_ms critical_threshold_ms persistence_minutes use_case
| sort 0 -peak_latency_ms endpoint volume
description: Monitors Windows LogicalDisk read and write response time from Perfmon. It converts the documented seconds-per-operation counters to milliseconds, calculates per-volume one-minute averages, and reports two consecutive breached minutes. The search uses Microsoft's general Windows Server warning and critical values while retaining enough timing and sample context for responders to verify the condition.
value: Sustained storage latency can slow applications even when capacity remains available. A volume-specific, persistence-aware signal helps operations teams start with the affected host and volume, compare workload and storage evidence, and avoid paging on a single transient sample or on an unrelated queue counter.
implementation: Collect the exact LogicalDisk read/write latency counters from every governed Windows host at 60 seconds or faster with stable English counter names. Validate seconds-to-milliseconds conversion and source completeness, schedule the fixed five-minute window after measured ingest delay, test strict 25/50 ms boundaries and adjacent-minute persistence, then route findings with application, virtualization, and storage ownership context. Treat absent samples as telemetry-health findings.
visualization: Use a per-volume timechart with separate read and write millisecond series and horizontal 25/50 ms reference lines; a table showing host, volume, peak, averages, sample counts, breach interval, delay, owner, and source health; and a completeness panel for expected hosts/counters/minutes. Do not graph queue length on the latency axis or merge logical and physical instances without an explicit mapping.

schema: Windows Perfmon LogicalDisk event samples with exact counter, instance, Value-in-seconds, and event/index-time contract
dataModelAcceleration: The Splunk Add-on maps `Perfmon:LogicalDisk` to Performance, whose Storage dataset defines `read_latency` and `write_latency` in milliseconds. Use the CIM variant only after field-level parity proves host, mount, units, minute grain, `_Total` exclusion, latency values, and acceleration freshness. The raw search remains authoritative for counter names, original seconds, sample counts, and ingest-health investigation.

knownFalsePositives:
1. **Approved backup or maintenance load** — backup, antivirus, patching, indexing, database maintenance, volume snapshots, and storage migration can produce genuine sustained latency. Correlate exact time, volume, workload, and approved change; do not suppress unrelated periods.

2. **Storage-path transition** — planned failover, live migration, multipath change, array maintenance, or cloud-disk tier operation can raise real latency while service remains acceptable. The owner must provide the bounded window and affected volumes.

3. **General threshold versus workload SLO** — Microsoft's 25/50 ms values are general Windows troubleshooting guidance. A latency-sensitive application may be harmed below 25 ms, while an owner may accept higher latency for an archival workload. Keep application/vendor SLO monitoring separate; do not relabel this rule as an SLO breach.

4. **Logical-to-physical ambiguity** — several logical volumes can share one physical disk, virtual disk, SAN LUN, cloud disk, or array path. A valid logical-volume finding may appear on multiple volumes and does not identify the failed component.

5. **Duplicate collection route** — direct and WEF-like relay patterns, duplicate Perfmon stanzas, or checkpoint/replay can bias averages. The SPL removes exact same-time/value duplicates, but source health must investigate route-level duplication.

6. **Counter locale or alias drift** — non-English names, changed source mode, or extraction differences can cause missing or mismatched fields rather than a false latency value. Use `useEnglishOnly=true` where supported and alert on completeness.

7. **Sampling and bucket edge** — a workload crossing minute/window boundaries may create or avoid an adjacent pair. Review raw samples and use a longer owner-approved trend for diagnosis; do not widen an alert retrospectively.

8. **Virtualized or cached storage semantics** — guest-observed LogicalDisk latency includes the Windows I/O path visible to the guest and may differ from hypervisor, host, cache, or array measures. Correlate all layers before assigning cause.

Suppress only by exact host and volume, documented reason, owner, approved start, and finite expiry in the alerting layer. Never suppress collection-health reporting, broad host classes, or all backup hours without confirming the affected volume and risk.
detectionType: Two consecutive one-minute logical-disk latency threshold breaches
reviewer: Source-backed editorial review; production owner and Windows/storage SME validation pending

cost.search_load_notes: Five-minute bounded aggregation over two LogicalDisk counters; ingest cost scales with hosts, volumes, counters, and sample interval.

detailedImplementation:
## Prerequisites and authoritative contract

Assign Windows, application/service, virtualization, storage, Splunk, and incident owners. Inventory every governed host and logical volume, including mount/drive instance, workload, service owner, criticality, maintenance/backup windows, virtualization layer, physical/LUN/cloud-disk mapping, storage tier, vendor support boundary, and application latency objective. The primary contract is deliberately narrow: two consecutive complete one-minute buckets in which the average `Avg. Disk sec/Read` or `Avg. Disk sec/Write` is strictly greater than 25 ms. Microsoft publishes <15 ms healthy, >25 ms warning, and >50 ms critical guidance for Windows logical and physical disk read/write latency and advises investigating periods over one minute. This implementation interprets that guidance as two adjacent one-minute buckets and labels a pair critical when either minute is strictly above 50 ms. Record that interpretation as local policy; it is not a storage-vendor guarantee.

Microsoft defines disk latency as elapsed time from creation through completion of an I/O request. `Avg. Disk sec/Read` and `/Write` are seconds per operation, so multiply only those values by 1,000. `Current Disk Queue Length` is an instantaneous raw queue-depth value, while average queue length and transfer/byte counters have other semantics. Never multiply them by 1,000 or place them on a millisecond axis. Exclude `_Total` from the primary result to retain an actionable volume; use it only for context.

## Step 1 — Configure and prove collection

Install a supported Splunk Enterprise or Universal Forwarder on each Windows collection host and deploy Splunk Add-on for Microsoft Windows through reviewed configuration management. The Splunk platform uses Windows PDH through `splunk-perfmon.exe` for local Perfmon inputs. Create the local stanza under `Splunk_TA_windows/local/inputs.conf`; do not edit the add-on's `default` directory. A representative event-index stanza is:

```ini
[perfmon://LogicalDisk]
object = LogicalDisk
counters = Avg. Disk sec/Read; Avg. Disk sec/Write; Avg. Disk sec/Transfer; Disk Reads/sec; Disk Writes/sec; Disk Read Bytes/sec; Disk Write Bytes/sec; Avg. Disk Queue Length; Current Disk Queue Length
instances = *
interval = 60
mode = single
useEnglishOnly = true
index = perfmon
disabled = 0
```

Validate the exact supported setting names against the deployed Splunk version and add-on. Sixty seconds is the maximum interval for this two-adjacent-minute implementation; a shorter interval supplies multiple samples per bucket. Confirm with Windows Performance Monitor or `Get-Counter` that both exact English latency counters and intended instances exist. Compare simultaneous Windows and Splunk samples, accounting for poll boundaries, and prove `Value` is seconds before applying the conversion. Confirm `host`, `source` or `sourcetype`, `counter`, `instance`, numeric `Value`, `_time`, and `_indextime` from raw events. Do not assume metric-index field shape is identical; create a separately tested `mstats` implementation when using metric indexes.

Build independent collection health from the governed inventory. Report missing host, volume, counter, or minute; stale/future `_time`; p95/p99 indexing delay; blank/nonnumeric/negative Value; locale/case drift; unexpected `_Total`-only collection; duplicate stanza/route; interval drift; forwarder/input disabled; and abrupt sample-count change. Silence can mean idle storage only if expected zero-valued samples still arrive. Preserve deployment-server class, configuration checksum, forwarder/add-on version, restart/change record, and health results.

## Step 2 — Create and understand the search

Save sidecar `spl` verbatim as `windows_logical_disk_sustained_latency`. Run every five minutes. At 12:15, `earliest=-10m@m latest=-5m@m` covers 12:05 through but not including 12:10, allowing five minutes for ingestion. Measure actual p99 delay; move both bounds together to preserve nonoverlap and run a separately governed late-data reconciliation if required.

The base search accepts the documented event sourcetype/source and only the two exact latency counters. It normalizes host and instance, rejects `_Total`, null, and negative values, and removes exact duplicate same-time samples. It converts seconds to milliseconds, bins into complete minutes, and calculates separate read/write averages and sample counts. `minute_peak_ms` selects the available direction's maximum without inventing a missing value. Values must be strictly >25 ms. After sorting by endpoint/volume/time, `streamstats` compares each breached minute with the preceding breached minute; exactly 60 seconds proves adjacency. A single spike or separated breaches cannot alert. The final row gives the affected host/volume, two-minute-or-longer interval, peak, directional averages, samples, thresholds, and indexing times.

A critical result means the pair peak is strictly >50 ms; exactly 50 ms remains warning, and exactly 25 ms does not breach. This follows the comparison wording encoded here and must be boundary-tested. The search does not claim that every sample in a minute exceeded the threshold, only that the minute average did. Keep diagnostic searches for transfer rate, bytes, queues, process I/O, physical disks, Windows storage events, application response, hypervisor, and array telemetry separate so their units and grain remain clear.

## Step 3 — Validate thresholds, persistence, and units

Implement fixed fixtures described in `controlTest`. Test 0, 0.015, 0.025, 0.025001, 0.050, and 0.050001 seconds and assert 0, 15, 25, 25.001, 50, and 50.001 ms after conversion. Test read-only, write-only, and both directions; multiple samples per minute; a single breach; adjacent and nonadjacent breaches; `_Total`; null, text, negative, and missing values; duplicate same-time samples; different volumes on one host; same volume name on two hosts; late/future events; interval gaps; and rerun idempotence. Assert that queue depth and transfer-rate counters never enter the latency calculation.

In an isolated Windows/storage lab, generate an owner-approved bounded I/O workload without damaging production data. Capture Windows Performance Monitor, Splunk raw samples, application response, LogicalDisk and PhysicalDisk rates/queues, process I/O operations, virtual/storage-layer measurements, and source health. Increase load only within lab safety limits; the goal is field/unit/persistence proof, not forcing hardware failure. Verify that one high sample does not fire, two adjacent high minute averages do, and removing collection creates a health finding rather than a latency result.

Measure sample completeness, duplicate rate, ingest delay, search runtime/skips, alert delivery, result volume, and host/volume cardinality. Keep `status=draft` until Windows, application, storage, virtualization, Splunk, and incident owners approve the collection contract, Microsoft-threshold interpretation, fixtures, health monitoring, dashboard, routing, and response.

## Step 4 — Operationalize without overclaiming

Dashboard separate read and write latency series in milliseconds with 25/50 ms lines. Add workload/change overlays and a table with host, volume, breach interval, peak, directional averages, counts, delay, source health, application owner, storage mapping, and restricted raw drilldown. Show queue, throughput, IOPS, and application/hypervisor/array measures on separate labeled panels. Never combine unlike units on one axis.

Route warning to the service/storage owner and critical according to locally approved availability policy. Alert title should say `Sustained Windows logical-disk latency above general threshold`; do not say `disk failing`, `SAN outage`, or `application unavailable`. Throttle by exact host and volume only after preserving new peaks and recurring intervals. Any maintenance suppression requires exact scope, reason, approver, start, and expiry; source-health alerts remain unsuppressed.

Responder sequence:
1. Verify raw counter names, instance, Value, seconds-to-ms conversion, adjacent minute buckets, duplicate handling, event/index times, and collection health.
2. Confirm the logical volume and map it at event time to workload, virtual disk, physical disk, path, LUN/array/cloud disk, tier, and owner.
3. Check application response and change/backup/patch/AV/database activity; a genuine latency event can still be planned.
4. Compare read/write/transfer latency, IOPS, bytes, queue depth, free capacity, process I/O, PhysicalDisk, Windows/storage errors, hypervisor contention, path/multipath state, and vendor telemetry.
5. Compare measured demand and latency with application objectives and vendor-rated limits. Do not infer saturation from queue length alone.
6. Classify transient load, sustained demand beyond capacity, host/driver/filter issue, virtual contention, path/fabric/array problem, cloud-tier behavior, collection defect, or unresolved; engage the correct owner.

Never automatically stop a process/service, take a disk offline, detach/remount a volume, fail over storage, migrate a VM, change queue depth/cache/tier, reboot, or isolate a host from this result. Those actions can corrupt data or broaden an outage. Follow approved storage/application procedures with backups, integrity checks, rollback, and coordinated evidence preservation.

## Step 5 — Troubleshoot and close

- **No data:** verify the host is governed, forwarder/service and deployment class, stanza enabled, Windows counter availability, exact index/RBAC, source/sourcetype, locale, add-on extraction, and `_internal` input errors.
- **Only `_Total`:** inspect `instances=*`, Windows instance visibility, permissions, and source mode. Do not alert on `_Total` as if it were a volume.
- **Values 1,000 times wrong:** compare raw Windows and Splunk samples. Multiply the two seconds-per-operation counters once; CIM latency fields are already milliseconds.
- **No adjacent pair:** inspect minute boundaries, input interval, missing samples, ingest delay, and whether breaches were actually consecutive. Do not weaken persistence to hide collection gaps.
- **Too many alerts:** validate duplicate routes, actual workload, exact instance cardinality, threshold comparisons, and planned activity. Do not add a broad host suppression.
- **CIM differs:** verify the Storage dataset tags, host/mount mapping, read/write latency units, acceleration range/freshness, `_Total` handling, and minute grain. Use raw events until parity is demonstrated.
- **Windows and array differ:** align clocks, logical-to-physical mapping, cache/layer visibility, sample interval, aggregation, and direction. The measurements observe different layers and need not match exactly.

Close only with documented cause and owner; healthy collection; confirmed volume/layer mapping; workload and application-impact assessment; completed repair/capacity/change or accepted bounded behavior; restored latency under the applicable objective; and no unexplained recurrence during an owner-approved observation interval. Retention follows local policy; no fixed day count is asserted.
grandmaExplanation: We watch how long each Windows drive takes to finish reading and writing. If it stays slow for more than a brief moment, we show the team which computer and drive need investigation without claiming the drive is broken.
hardware: Windows client or server hosts exposing the LogicalDisk performance object. The logical instance can map to local media, a virtual disk, Storage Spaces, a cluster/shared volume, SAN LUN, or cloud block storage; retain an authoritative mapping before assigning a physical cause.
